items.question: Why do you think the science of LLMs needs to go beyond describing their capabilities as “fractal intelligence”?
items.object: Fractal intelligence and the limits of LLM reasoning
items.answer: I think Andrej Karpathy basically was saying LLMs have fractal intelligence. What the fractal intelligence is, basically, we don't know when they work, they work; when they don't, they don't. That's fractal intelligence. Still, we had nothing like this before, but part of the science of LLMs has to be to say something more than fractal intelligence, saying, here is the level to which you can depend on the results. There are, in reasoning, in logic, ways of formally characterizing the limits of reasoning, like limited depth, limited lookahead reasoning, and so on. None of them seem to work for LLMs. The question then is what would work? We have to figure that out.

items.question: Why do you agree with the view that the bitter lesson is over and efficiency is going to matter?
items.object: Efficiency after the bitter lesson
items.answer: I've been arguing this for a long time too. Think about the following thing. The first time when we sent humans to the moon, cost was not a consideration. We want to show that we can do it. NASA was the one which is doing it. The second time and the third—for space as well as the moon, the second and third time, etc., may be okay, but by now it's Elon Musk sending people to space and supposedly possibly to Mars too, because the cost matters, right? Essentially, once it's been done, then you start caring about the cost that you're paying. And computer science is actually quite a bit about the unsexy parts of cost, just as it is about doing things that haven't been done before.

items.question: How do you assess autoregressive large language models as reasoning tools?
items.object: Autoregressive large language models
items.answer: I think of large language models as the autoregressive token-by-token prediction models, which are pre-trained for that. And they also do that at inference time. From my perspective, those did not have the reasoning abilities. They are amazing in supporting creative work, where they can give you ideas and you can run with them, and they will give you an answer as soon as you hit return. But they are not guaranteed to be correct.

items.question: How do you understand why adding “Let's think step by step” to an LLM reasoning prompt can improve its answer?
items.object: Chain-of-thought prompting and the phrase “Let's think step by step”
items.answer: An idea I find very interesting is: it's been known from day one that if you are trying to give a reasoning task to an LLM as a prompt, and then it gives a completion and you check its completion whether it contains the solution, the probability of that happening in general can be made higher if you can find the right kind of prompt augmentation. So in addition to your reasoning thing, some magical tokens that you add, and that seems to increase the probability. And this has been seen in multiple scenarios. Originally, this idea has been bandied about as chain of thought. And the very first version of that essentially is the zeroth-order chain of thought, where the magical token will always be the same one, irrespective of the task: 'Let's think step by step.' And that sort of worked, partly because the human data had those specific types of tokens. And so LLM outputs that, and then that jogs its pattern matching to actually pick up other solutions, so on and so on.

items.question: How do you assess chain-of-thought prompting as a way to improve an LLM's reasoning?
items.object: Chain-of-thought prompting
items.answer: Chain of thought by itself has, again, problems, just as verification has problems. In fact, this NeurIPS we had a paper called 'Chain of Thoughtlessness,' but basically by itself it has problems. But as part of the toolbox of increasing the time spent during inference time before you blurt out one answer, chain of thought together with the sort of picking from many samples has shown some promise. One variation of that, and in fact that is something that I've been pushing more recently, is: originally chain of thought was kind of confused with—it might be anthropomorphic. We tend to tell ourselves, okay, let me do it this way, etc., and people are hoping that LLMs are doing the same thing. Mostly they were just kind of imitating whatever 'let's think step by step' data they had found in the training data. But somehow people thought if you kind of make them imitate human thinking, then maybe they will do better. Another idea, essentially, is you realize that it's just a magical token that you are trying to add, and you just have to figure out what's the right magical token. And it's sort of a Skolem function. You're trying to figure out a task-specific, LM-specific magical token that increases the probability. This is a learning problem. It's an extra learning problem.

items.question: What account of how OpenAI's o1 works would make its reasoning capabilities make sense to you?
items.object: A reinforcement-learning explanation of OpenAI's o1 reasoning model
items.answer:
Again, as you know, O1—nobody knows. They don't want to tell what they're doing. But my best guess as to what O1 might be doing is going again with this prompt-augmentation idea. But the question, of course, is where are these prompt augmentations coming from? We talked about the first one: prompt augmentation for everything. Second is human-given prompt augmentation, which is chain of thought. The third is the synthetic derivational traces that sort of give these tokens. But none of them really make too much sense. A much better idea is, if you are saying, what should I be telling myself to improve my outcome, it's a kind of RL problem. Imagine an AlphaGo agent. It's sitting there and thinking, what actions should I do one after another such that my win probability increases? So it does a whole bunch of these board actions. And then at some point it gets a signal saying you won the game or you lost the game, and then you do this a gazillion times. You can then bring this reasoning back through the sequential decisions, computing the Q-values, like under what board positions or what actions are worth doing.

Now if you take the AlphaGo analogy and put it to LLMs, the LLM's board position is essentially the context window with the prompt and all the other stuff that you put on. And the action is this token that you are generating. So to make things simple, I would like to think of it as there's a big LM. Let's think of a GPT-4. There might be a small LM which has a reduced vocabulary. All it's trying to do is give these prompt augmentations that it tries. This will be given to this other LM in terms of its context. It gives extensions and then it tries one more. And then at some point it checks if the solution is correct. You could have actually generated huge numbers of synthetic examples beforehand, again using solvers. It's systematic solvers solving the planning problem, constraint satisfaction problems, and various sorts of problems, for which they have the problem and the answer. And then the LLM plus this prompt-augmentation engine is trying to solve it. And then if it happens to reach the correct solution, then you can propagate the thing back. This is RL in pseudo moves. If the prompt is about Go, the actions are not Go actions. They are essentially these prompt-augmentation tokens.

One nice thing, of course, is instead of learning the Q-values, one of the things you can do is change the weights of the smaller LM in the right ways, such that it puts out the right kinds of tokens given the context window. If you do this, you have gotten approximate Q-values. There is the LM training, followed by this humongous, costly post-training phase. At that point, you have O1 model, which is now ready for inference time. And at inference time, once again, they are doing inference time scaling, except now they have the Q-values. You can improve the Q-values by online MCT kinds of approaches, the kind of thing that AlphaGo did.

Essentially, you are doing something like an AlphaGo-style post-training phase, followed by an AlphaGo-style MCT online computation. And at that point, actually, I would think it could make sense. And not surprisingly, in our results, we found that for normal PlanBench, it does much better than the state-of-the-art LLMs, including Claude. But it has its own issues. It doesn't scale beyond the larger problems. It can make mistakes. It has problems with unsolvability. There are no guarantees about the solution, but it now makes more sense to me. Again, I don't know. I think this makes a reasonable way O1 can be working, and if it is the way it's working, for the first time I can make sense of how reasoning can emerge, because you are at least having the pseudo actions whose Q-values you are learning. And nobody ever said RL cannot do reasoning. RL can do reasoning. It's just that now I keep using the 'stone soup' analogy: you can make soup with stones if you start adding carrots and tomatoes and all that stuff. At that point of time it will still taste like soup. The question, of course, is who gets the credit?

items.question: How do you think the cost of o1-style reasoning changes the choice of AI systems?
items.object: The computational and financial costs of o1-style reasoning
items.answer:
One of the other interesting things is part of the mystique of LLMs was you write the prompt, you hit return, you get the answer, and it doesn't cost you too much. That was where everybody was using it. O1, with its post-training itself extremely costly, is not charging us for that, but they are charging us for the reasoning tokens, which you never see, but you pay for it. You just have to take their word that a huge number of reasoning tokens were generated, and they're going to make you pay for that. When we started playing with O1 Preview, when it came out, in two days we spent like $8,000. In fact, I had to get special permission from the university because they normally don't reimburse beyond a certain thing unless you have separate permission.

As far as I could tell, at least in academia, very few people have actually been doing experiments evaluating O1 because it actually costs a lot. So one of the interesting things is you can do reasoning, but the usual computational complexity issues that we blithely forgot in the era of autoregressive leaps will come back. We are hoping that somehow complexity will disappear. Because if you want to improve accuracy, you have to actually do reasoning. And this is pseudo reasoning, in my view, but still it costs. And that becomes an interesting question of when is it useful to use a general-purpose system versus a hybrid general-special-purpose system versus an extremely specialized solver, something that we haven't talked about before, but now it will become costlier, at least for industries. In fact, there's this whole movement about compound AI systems, and that's basically the kind of thing that people think about very shortly after O1 was released.

items.question: How do you interpret O1's performance on the PlanBench planning problems you tested?
items.object: O1's performance on PlanBench
items.answer: What is objectively verifiable is we did test O1 on the same PlanBench problems, and they did quite well on Blocks World. I mean, I think Claude already had 66. These things were like 99 or something. They basically saturated. More impressively, they did better on the mystery domain. And, given what I explained about the possibility that they are training themselves with synthetic data, maybe they have unintentionally trained on the mystery domain which we have available outside. items.question: Why do you regard O1 as an approximate reasoner rather than a retriever?
items.object: O1 as an approximate reasoner rather than a retriever
items.answer: It's based a lot more on my reconstruction of what they could potentially be doing, which is they are sort of doing reinforcement-learning-based post-training as well as online Q-value updates, and using pseudo-action moves. I call them pseudo-action moves because you could do RL for just normal Go or any specific board games. This one is just language games, where the game basically is there's a language context window and there is a prompt augmentation and there is a new context, new completion, and then one more prompt augmentation. This is what they call this string of chains of thought, but that's basically adding bunches of prompt augmentation and then seeing what happens at the end. And then if it winds up being correct, in the sense that it contains the correct solution for your training data, then that's sort of like AlphaGo getting a victory win signal after a bunch of moves, and then it just needs to do credit-blame assignment for the moves. And that's what RL is essentially good at doing. And if you are doing that, it's reasoning, and it's approximate reasoning because it's not actually problem-specific actions. It is problem-independent. These language prompt actions.

items.question: How do you understand the roles of post-training and inference-time computation in OpenAI's O1?

items.question: Why do you prefer formal definitions of reasoning when evaluating AI systems that will be deployed?

I try to avoid getting into this question of what is human reasoning, because that is a big mess. Cognitive scientists don't know it. We don't know it. Psychologists don't know it. items.question: Why do you find the argument that LLMs must be reasoning because they are not merely retrieving unsatisfactory?

So there can be a whole universe of things between retrieval and what I would consider reasoning that still won't be considered reasoning, as far as I'm concerned, because there are no sorts of guarantees. First of all, everybody always knew that LLMs are not databases, right? So they don't retrieve, essentially; they actually have a hard time memorizing and retrieving. When they memorize it, it's not by deliberation. It doesn't happen deliberately. It happens fortuitously. It's surprising that sometimes they wind up memorizing long passages, because essentially everybody agrees that there are some kind of n-gram models rather than databases in the way they are trained. No, that's not making sense because, again, you have to subject it to what you would consider as evaluations for sound reasoning procedures, and they fail just as easily as before. items.answer: I do want to say that there is a distinction between factual tasks and reasoning tasks, right? LLMs have been used for both. For the reasoning stuff, for arithmetic and so on, I would expect these are the kinds of things where the exact results don't exist. And so I would also be equally troubled by the fact that people have shown that if you take something like multiplication—this is way before all this Laura's work—they tend to be correct in multiplications for popular digits and less correct for non-popular digits. But the fact that it gets to be correct for popular digits and not for some other digits is a particularly interesting thing to me.

items.question: How do you assess O1's handling of unsolvable planning problems?
items.object: O1's handling of unsolvable planning problems
items.answer: One thing that I've looked at is the Twitter exchanges about people, the usual suspects, trying the various things on them. One of the things we saw in O1 Preview, and it looks like O1 is still doing it, is they are good at digging to try and explain why their answer is the correct answer. One of the funny things was I used this one particular three-block stacking example, which is unsolvable. And in fact, this showed up in the New York Times as an example of why GPT-4o fails on that. And when O1 Preview came out, Noam Brown actually—one of the things in his long tweet was Rav said this in an ACL talk, that this problem can be solved. And O1 Preview actually does solve this instance. And so this is good. Now people have actually said that O1 gets the wrong answer. Multiple people have seen this; people have posted the screenshots. It gets the wrong answer, but it argues with you as to why the answer it is giving is still possibly correct. In this particular problem, there is no way of actually solving it without moving C, and it turns out that it gives an answer where actually C moves because of gravity, it will fall down, and then it tries to argue with you that there are games where people will say that unless you are intentionally moving C, if the natural process makes it fall, it's not considered moving. That's a very interesting thing that we have seen in O1 Preview too, when we'll give it an unsolvable instance. Which, by the way, normal LMs just die with unsolvable instances because they have been RL'd to death. They think that if you give a problem to them, there must be an answer. So they'll give you something. And for some unsolvable problems, this is why this was the unsolvable instance that I showed to GPT-4 before. O1 Preview actually solves more of them correctly. That's a credit to it. That's why it's actually a more approximate reasoning model, LRM in my view, than LM. But on the other hand, when it gives a solution for an unsolvable instance, it will argue with you that it is still actually right. And so I made this joke in the Strawberry paper that we have gone from hallucinations to gaslighting.

items.question: What concerns you about the relationship between O1's explanations and its reasoning?
items.object: The relationship between O1's explanations and its reasoning
items.answer: Colin Fraser, I believe, one of these guys on Twitter who keeps playing with his models, said he gave the surgeon problem, the classical surgeon one, the boy getting into an accident, and O1 Pro said the surgeon basically does all this whole thing. This is a classical puzzle that brings gender stereotypes into account, et cetera, and then gives the answer that the right way to think about it is. This is the puzzle where the mother and the boy are driving, the mother dies, and the doctor says, 'I can't operate on the boy.' So it actually changes the puzzle, and still O1 apparently says we should realize that the doctor is the second mother of the boy, and it will try to argue that position. So interestingly, overthinking and actually trying to dig down is kind of a—actually, one of the interesting questions that we don't know, again, we haven't played with this, is to what extent is its explanation and its reasoning connected? In humans this is—I mean, I'm not trying to anthropomorphize what it's doing. It's just if there are two different phases, phase one comes up with a solution, and phase two needs to explain it. If it doesn't have to look at what it did to get to the solution, the explanation is just dig my heels in and try to say the solution is correct. People trying to do that sometimes will come to some solution and then try to come up with an explanation as to why what we did might be right. This is something LMs had this problem with to begin with, because they completely assumed these are different things. And I'm always worried about LMs' explanations. LMs seem to be even more sophisticated at this sometimes, but it's mostly anecdotal. I haven't really done systematic studies on this.

items.answer: First of all, O1 Pro just came, I think, last week. And this was exam week for me. We haven't spent any money yet on O1 Pro. items.question: How do you understand O1's reasoning abilities in relation to your reservations about autoregressive language models?
items.object: O1's reasoning abilities and the definition of language models
items.answer: My point is there are two different ways of thinking about it. One is it's not the LMs which became that. So how you define LMs has to be some discussion that we should have. I keep talking about the stone soup metaphor, not because I want to play down the importance of O1. It's a great thing. But you do have to decide who you want to give credit to if you are arguing part of my reservations about reasoning abilities of LMs, where there were autoregressive teacher-forced training things, and that was true from GPT-2.5 all the way to GPT-4o. OpenAI knows this. OpenAI knows it enough that they no longer call it GPT O1. It's called O1. It's like a completely different model. All you can say is that it was done by some of the same people that also developed LLMs, but we can't define LLMs to be whatever it is that OpenAI is producing. We have to have theoretical definitions. My sense is autoregressive LLMs still have all the problems, but all the advantages, because they're very fast. They're amazing fast system ones. And O1 is a reasoning model because it actually adds reasoning post-training as well as reasoning inference, which nobody said will not be doable. It's great still that they are able to do it in a very general sense, but I don't think there was any argument that AI systems were able to do reasoning. After all, AlphaGo is basically a reasoning system. It was just a deep and narrow reasoning system. And the question was, is a more general, broader, but not as shallow as LMs, a good step in the right direction? But it doesn't change what I thought about LMs, which is the autoregressive models are different, and they have advantages that O1 lacks.

items.question: How do you evaluate LLM Modulo as an alternative to O1 on reasoning problems?
items.object: LLM Modulo and the cost of reasoning
items.answer: One of the things we learned in the Strawberry paper, 'Planning in Strawberry Fields,' is that computer science is eventually about efficiency and cost too, right? If you are giving a particular instance of the problem to O1 and you pay this many dollars, versus you give the same instance to the LLM with a verifier in this inference-time-scaling approach, what I would call LLM Modulo, which is a general approach that we have been pushing, where it uses an autoregressive LLM to generate many candidates and an external verifier, or even an LLM-based verifier or a learned verifier, to check, that can actually be cheaper than O1 just doing one candidate with the same accuracy. That becomes interesting because part of the interesting thing about human civilization is, on one hand, we are general-purpose reasoners, but on the other hand, we also know that every job requires a tool. The fact that we are doing everything that a particular specialized tool does can be extremely inefficient in terms of the time that we are spending. That is going to be the case for these reasoning models to some extent, because O1 actually costs quite a bit right now. How much that is going to change is anybody's guess.

items.question: Why do you agree with the claim that “the bitter lesson is over and efficiency is going to matter” in AI?
items.object: The claim that the bitter lesson is over and efficiency will matter in AI
items.answer: I completely agree with that. I've been arguing this for a long time too. Think about the following thing: the first time when we sent humans to the moon, cost was not a consideration. We want to show that we can do it. NASA was the one which is doing it. The second time and the third—for space as well as the moon—may be okay, but by now it's Elon Musk sending people to space and supposedly possibly to Mars too, because the cost matters, right? Essentially, once it's been done, then you start caring about the cost that you're paying. And computer science is quite a bit about the unsexy parts of cost, just as it is about doing things that haven't been done before. We are now in the second phase where we are going to care about how much am I spending in terms of the pre-training costs, in terms of the inference costs, and are there better approaches that I can be using? This has been the case with computer science before too, and it just became less of an issue for a while because LLMs were system ones, because there was no inference-time cost at all. Even though the pre-training was very costly, inference time was very cheap. And so we didn't have to worry about it. Now we will worry about it.

items.question: How do you understand the trade-off between specialized classical planners and a general-purpose model like O1 Preview on your PlanBench problems?
items.object: The trade-off between classical planners and O1 Preview on PlanBench
items.answer: One of the funny things, the elephant in the room for our PlanBench problems on O1 Preview, was that the normal classical planners that are meant to solve these problems solve them in such a small fraction of the cost. They work on our laptops and solve all the problems with 100% guarantees. I realize they're completely specialized only for that problem, and then on the other hand you have this very general-purpose thing which has cost as well as inaccuracies. We start worrying about the trade-off. What level in this generality-cost spectrum are you going to find home? That is going to be a very important thing. items.question: How do you distinguish using large language and reasoning models as personal assistants from deploying them as autonomous systems that make decisions for end users?
items.object: Human-in-the-loop assistance versus autonomous uses of large language and reasoning models
items.answer:
One distinction I want to point out is these two notions of users of these kinds of models. When you do a subscription model, $20 or $200, I would argue that that is by definition human in the loop, with the model being an assistant to you. And it's a very different way of evaluation, where you were unhappy with the previous model because it was wasting more of your time and it's not worth it for you. This one was helping in whatever you were doing, and you are happy with that. That's one particular type. In general, I've always thought that large language models and Large Reasoning Models—there's no question that they are intelligence amplifiers. There's no question on that part. If you want to use it, you use it, and people are able to find uses for that. That's great.

The part I'm talking more about, and that's where most of our work has been, is there would be scenarios where these become the end-user-facing systems, where they will make the decisions. They will just say, this is the answer, and then you're going to execute this plan. The robot will execute this plan. This is the travel plan for which I will buy the tickets. You don't get to come back in and say, 'Oh, I don't like this travel plan.' That's what you do in the subscription model. But the one I'm talking about, basically API access, is what people—all the startups trying to build additional tools on top of these models—are going to give specific autonomous functionality. And that's where I'm talking about the actual computational cost versus benefit for a certain level of accuracy.

I have no question at all in my mind that all LLMs and definitely also LRMs are just great intelligence amplifiers. But that's not my worry. My worry has always been that people are trying to put this in end-user-facing situations where they'll actually make the decisions, and some executor just executes it without pushing back. When that happens, the guarantees matter; the brittleness of the reasoning matters. If you are in the loop, you will never blindly just use the assistant's ideas. You'll be the one the buck stops with. That's a very different way of using LMs than LMs being the ones that the patient talks to. There is no doctor between the LM or LRM and the patient, in which case their accuracy matters, and their cost in getting to a certain level of accuracy matters. These are two very different uses, and I'm much more interested in the second use than the first use.

items.question: How do you assess the idea of having a neural network generate solutions directly instead of generating code that produces the solutions?
items.object: Generating code versus directly generating solutions with neural networks
items.answer:
So to be honest, I haven't followed that work as closely. My answer is somewhat slightly more generic. I would be surprised. I would have the same bias toward generating higher-level code that generates the solutions. This has always been the conceit of computer science. I don't actually know specifically the work that you are referring to in terms of just going back and directly going for the solutions, because honestly, in the context of inference-time scaling, one interesting question is you generate loads and loads of candidates. The candidates can be either direct solution candidates or code candidates, either way, and then you still have to have a verifier. If it's code, you need a code verifier. If you have a solution, you need a solution verifier. One interesting question is where is this verifier coming from?

One of the more effective ideas we've been pursuing is you can essentially generate verifiers now. There are symbolic verifiers that might be there for specific things, and we can use that in modulo-style frameworks, but you could also use learned verifiers where you learn discriminatively what is a solution and what is not a solution. A third idea is generate the code for the verifier and then correct it. In fact, for us, it seems promising. We are working on some things that are going to come out soon.

I still think, especially in the context of LLMs, one of the things they're actually good at doing is outputting code as well as solutions. The code can output lots and lots of classes of solutions that can be verified, and so if you correct it once then it will work for a longer time, in a sense. items.question: How do you understand the trade-off between having a neural network guess a solution directly and having it generate a Python program that produces the solution?
items.object: Direct solution generation versus Python program generation by neural networks
items.answer: Interestingly, to me, again, it depends very much on the space of solution configurations versus the space of code configurations. There are many problems where solutions might be of less, quote unquote, syntactic complexity, and a neural network that can kind of guess a string may not be able to guess something that looks like a syntactically correct Python program, right? LLMs actually can do the latter. So it is interesting that if you can do that, and if you still go back to neural networks to directly guess the solution, it might be a more useful step. items.object: The “Chain of Thoughtlessness” paper
items.answer: When we wrote it, it was like, it can't follow procedures, so I should be able to show it. items.question: Why are you skeptical that chain-of-thought prompting teaches large language models to generalize procedures?
items.object: Procedure generalization through chain-of-thought prompting
items.answer: I mean, that's basically because it doesn't quite know how to generalize. And so I kind of made that point: essentially, you have to give it examples for word problems, give it examples for seven-word problems, give examples of nine-word problems, etc., and then try to improve it. Whereas the conceit people have is when you say this, they'll say, “Oh, it must be doing procedure generalization.” I'm skeptical only because of having some additional background. One of the things is John McCarthy, who is one of the founding fathers, the guy who coined the name artificial intelligence, basically said the holy grail of AI is an Advice Taker program, and Advice Taker is AI-complete. If chain of thought is able to make LLMs take advice, that would be pretty impressive. I went in thinking that there have to be holes there. That is where that fish, one fish, two fish thing comes in.

items.question: How do you think human intelligibility should matter when designing prompt augmentations for large language models?
items.object: Human intelligibility of LLM prompt augmentations
items.answer: To me, the more interesting thing is anthropomorphizing LLMs and trying to think of them as alien entities for which arbitrary prompt augmentations can generate good behavior. One example is jailbreaks and LLMs: you give a normal prompt and this particular carefully constructed learned sequence. The original paper from his group shows that sequence makes no sense to humans, but it will make most LLMs provide a deterministic behavior, like saying “got you” or something of that kind. Essentially that should tell us that they are not seeing language. So prompt augmentations don't have to make sense to humans in the loop, and that's okay. In some sense, looking at things that made sense to humans gave the false impression that somehow LLMs are doing things like we do, but that's not the way it is. Might as well go with what they can do and optimize directly, which is what the inference-time-scaling and post-training methods seem to be doing.

items.question: How do you reconcile your support for compound language-model systems with your criticism of claims that a single model can do everything?
items.object: Compound language-model systems and claims about single-model capabilities
items.answer: I'm a big believer in that whole direction. But there are some people who don't want to believe that, the usual LM aficionados. It's a very interesting thing that OpenAI was at pains to point out that O1 Preview was a model, not a system. It's not me and you saying it; it's them saying it. They would like to say there is this one-size-fits-all model that will do it. And so it is reasonable to take their word for that. items.question: How do you understand OpenAI's preference for a single general-purpose AI model?
items.object: OpenAI's preference for a single general-purpose AI model
items.answer: I think there was a reason. To some extent I can understand. In a sense, it would be this sort of anthropomorphizing again: we only have one brain. So it would be nice if what we are trying to do would somehow be this one-size-fits-all general system. But at the same time, there is this issue: whatever I do, I want to provide guarantees, safety, so that it can be used in safety-critical systems. The problem is modern AI, neuroscience, and cognitive science are not one and the same, right? Everybody understands that. Neural networks themselves are not really that well connected to the brain. They are biologically implausible. LLMs are definitely not, but there's nothing wrong with that. Just like we say, planes don't have to flap their wings. We don't try to make sense of planes and birds in the same sentence because they both fly. Other than that, the mechanics are different; the flight equations are not exactly the same things. That's going to be more the case with LMs too. As long as we realize that, it would be good. I think OpenAI originally—my sense is a bunch of these people were hoping they would get two birds with one stone: AI systems as well as understand how the brain works. I don't really think that part; nobody really believes it, honestly. You might use these systems to improve our understanding in actually doing neuroscience. In fact, I think Sung Kim says these systems help in doing neuroscience research, but they're not necessarily telling you how the brain works. So that's just speculation that might explain why OpenAI and some of these people are sticking to it.

items.question: How do you see the role of language models in compound AI systems?
items.object: The role of language models in compound AI systems
items.answer: The conversations I've been having on the sidelines at the conference: the companies, startups, etc., are already going much more into hybrid systems, much more into compound systems. That would basically not be a single system. But OpenAI is also slowly coming up with these fine-tuning models. They have RL fine-tuning stuff for your specific kinds of scenarios, etc. It would be interesting to see. Compound systems are very different: the individual role that the LM has to play is much less demanding. One of the fun things is we can do LM Modulo with normal LMs, or LM Modulo with O1. The generation of candidates is costlier, and we show in the Strawberry paper that we can further improve the performance of O1 Preview on some problems. Even though we couldn't change how much time it takes to think, we could improve its accuracy quite significantly just by calling it multiple times with better criticisms of the instance, the problems, and the answers it gave. That is still using them in a system. LMs themselves can be used in a system. But I think OpenAI itself just wants to call them models, up until now. Let's see what happens.
